extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and practicing journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the kinds of pressures (political, economic, legal, peer, audience, interest-group) that influence news selection and production, and the journalistic responses (fight back, give in, anticipatory avoidance) including standards for evidence and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / government pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct pressure from politicians and government officials on executives or journalists to alter or suppress coverage (example: the shortening/killing of a Watergate segment after pressure from Charles Colson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executives may or may not pass the pressure to editorial staff; political pressure is less effective when there is widespread public interest in a story. Attempts can backfire by creating additional news about the pressure itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic threats to the firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats aimed at the media corporation (loss of advertisers, revocation or nonrenewal of FCC licenses, cancellation of government contracts) intended to influence newsroom output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks are especially vulnerable because of FCC licensing and corporate government contracts; such threats may be implied rather than explicit and may be exerted through allies (e.g., urging supporters to apply for licenses or threatening to withdraw contracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigations as a pressure tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Government- or agency-initiated inquiries (e.g., congressional investigations) into news organizations or specific programs that impose costs and burdens on journalists and producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when investigations do not result in sanctions, they consume time and money, can erode network enthusiasm for exposés, and may lead to the departure ('extrusion') of individual journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal pressure: lawsuits, subpoenas, and searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of litigation, subpoenas for files/outtakes, or law-enforcement searches to restrain reporting, identify sources, or otherwise intimidate journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained legal action can void practical protections (e.g., source confidentiality), chill reporting, and force expensive legal defenses. Recent court rulings (as of the text) permitting newsroom searches or denying access to institutions can have far-reaching restrictive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience mobilization pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts by officials or critics to mobilize public opinion and mass complaint (letters, phone calls) to shame or pressure news organizations (example: Vice-President Agnew's 1969 speeches prompting ~100,000 contacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects depend on the existing sentiment of the audience and whether management publicly defends journalists; vocal audience pressure can chill journalists if it becomes sizable or is sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized campaigns by interest groups (letters, press conferences, public meetings) to protest perceived unfair or inaccurate coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pressure is effective when it secures political support, threatens advertisers or affiliates, or persuades journalists. News documentaries and entertainment programming are particular targets; powerless groups are usually ignored unless their claims are corroborated by more authoritative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer and professional criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure and evaluation from fellow journalists, media critics, and professional publications (e.g., Columbia Journalism Review) that review and judge news organizations and journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics employed by competitors are often distrusted; professional journals exert normative influence by condemning empirical sloppiness (unreliable sources, stereotypes, reliance on handouts, corruption) and praising energetic legwork, thoughtful analysis, persistence, and risk-taking. Favorable reviews contribute to prestige and can affect programming decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive responses: fighting back
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic strategies to resist pressure such as publicly asserting freedom of the press, rapidly speaking out against threats, and reporting attempts at pressure as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to autonomy draw on constitutional guarantees and public consensus; publicizing pressure can deter exertors. Journalists also sometimes ignore audience criticism that is constant and perceived as lacking bite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender/compromise: giving in
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of accommodation where journalists or organizations yield to pressure, often camouflaging the surrender (e.g., delayed resignations, after-the-fact apologies, altering future coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists tend to respond more to critics who can hurt them (advertisers, authoritative figures) and less to powerless critics; surrender may take the form of changed editorial practices, holding stories until more evidence accrues, or altering emphasis to avoid repeated criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory avoidance and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Preemptive actions taken to avoid foreseeable pressure, which can be built into routine practices and thus not perceived as censorship (e.g., avoiding certain story ideas, cooperating with powerful sources to stay in their good graces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include editorial choices influenced by advertisers, source relationships that skew toward official sources, and institutional practices (reviews, story selection rules) that reduce the likelihood of confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with power holders (advertisers, government, security officials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate collaboration with advertisers, government agencies, or other powerful actors to preserve goodwill, maintain access, or avoid sanctions (examples: postponing advertising that clashes with news, pre-publication reviews by lawyers or professionals, self-censorship on national security matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation may be motivated by civic concerns (national security), fear of regulation, desire for access or scoops, or executives' personal ties to government. While it can secure benefits, it may also compromise editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of evidence and empirical credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm that news stories must be based on convincing and legally defensible evidence, with higher evidentiary standards applied to controversial stories or those likely to provoke pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards tighten at higher organizational levels—top editors and executives demand more proof. Authoritative sources are accepted more readily; stories about powerful targets typically require stronger evidence than those about powerless groups. A taboo on 'unbelievable news' can lead to suppression even when some evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and foreign-law review practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional practice of subjecting potentially risky stories to legal review and, for international editions, tailoring text with foreign libel laws in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having lawyers on call and adjusting copy for foreign libel regimes preserves the organization legally but can influence phrasing, sourcing, and the decision to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive and ownership influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of founders, owners, and executives in shaping editorial choices through personal political activities, social ties, or corporate priorities (examples: owners using outlets to lobby for policies; executives with government roles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founders/owners historically may be more willing to use news organizations for political aims than appointed executives; executives' ties to government can chill journalists, since executives have immediate control over personnel and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lawsuits and legal harassment to punish or silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic deployment of libel suits and other litigation to harass journalists—forcing time-consuming, expensive defenses that can suppress controversial reporting, especially for outlets lacking resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when unsuccessful, suits can punish and deter; smaller or radical publications lacking legal funds may be driven out of existence, while large organizations may still become more cautious about risky projects.
